strengths: Well-motivated approach that tackles the known sample inefficiency of CVaR policy gradients by leveraging the dynamic programming properties of static VaR (quantiles).

Solid theoretical contributions, including the derivation of a new contraction Bellman operator for the state-only quantile value function, along with proofs for contraction and uniqueness of the fixed point.
An elegant mechanism to reduce the history-dependent optimal VaR policy to a Markovian policy class by tracking cumulative rewards, supported by theoretical justification (Propositions 3.3 and 3.4).
Strong empirical evaluation showing clear advantages over representative state-of-the-art baselines (such as RET-CAP, PCVaR-PG, and MIX) in three distinct risk-sensitive environments.
High clarity in presentation, featuring detailed pseudo-code (Algorithm 4), clear proof sketches, and comprehensive experimental details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The proposed algorithm introduces several additional hyperparameters (e.g., the trade-off parameter ω, its decay schedule, the number of quantiles I, and the soft quantile loss parameters ε and κ). The sensitivity of the algorithm to these parameters is not extensively evaluated.

There is a theoretical gap regarding convergence; while the paper proves that the optimal policy achieves the maximum of the objective, it remains an open question whether the iterative joint updates of the policy and value function starting from arbitrary initializations will converge.

Increased implementation complexity compared to standard policy gradient methods, as it requires maintaining and updating a monotonic quantile value network and tracking cumulative rewards to determine running quantile levels during both execution and learning.

strengths: Elegant core idea: Augmenting trajectory-based CVaR policy gradients (which suffer from high variance and sample inefficiency) with transition-based VaR policy gradients (which leverage recursive dynamic programming) is highly intuitive and mathematically sound since CVaR is the expectation of VaR over the tail.

Solid theoretical contributions: The paper successfully extends the framework of Hau et al. (2025) to state-value functions, proving contraction mapping properties (Proposition 3.1) and uniqueness of the fixed point (Proposition 3.2). Additionally, it theoretically validates how the history-dependent policy can be reduced to the Markovian policy class (Propositions 3.3 and 3.4).

Practical deep RL design: The authors address deep learning challenges such as quantile crossing by introducing a monotonic cumulative softplus parameterization, and leverage multi-step advantage estimation to improve gradient updates.

Convincing empirical results: The proposed CVaR-VaR method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines (such as RET-CAP and PCVaR-PG) in terms of sample efficiency, convergence speed, and risk-aversion across three diverse benchmarks (Maze, LunarLander, Inverted Pendulum).
weaknesses: Clarity on objective equivalence: Since the expected quantile term is mathematically equivalent to CVaR, the objective in Equation 7 is identical to the standard CVaR objective. Although briefly mentioned in the abstract, the paper should state this identity more explicitly in Section 3 to clarify that the improvement comes entirely from the gradient mixture (optimization process) rather than a modified objective.

Theoretical gap in joint convergence: As noted by the authors in Section 3.2, it remains an open question whether the joint iterative updates of the arbitrary policy and value function will converge to the optimal policy. While empirical success is demonstrated, more discussion on the theoretical implications or limitations of this joint optimization would be beneficial.

Sensitivity to hyperparameter scheduling: The trade-off parameter \omega requires manual scheduling (e.g., decaying linearly after 40% of iterations in LunarLander, or setting to 0 after 25% in Inverted Pendulum) to achieve optimal performance. The paper would be stronger with an ablation study demonstrating the sensitivity of the algorithm to different schedules or fixed values of \omega.

Finitely supported reward assumption: The theoretical derivations in Section A.2 assume finitely supported random rewards. The authors should briefly discuss how this assumption impacts continuous-reward domains common in deep RL.

strengths: An elegant and mathematically sound core idea: utilizing the equivalence between CVaR and the expectation of VaR over the tail to augment CVaR policy gradients with TD-style quantile gradients, allowing the use of all sampled data.

Solid theoretical contributions, including the derivation and contraction proof of a new Bellman operator for state-only quantile value functions, and showing how the optimal Markovian policy can be executed via cumulative reward tracking on the induced quantile value function.
Strong empirical performance on risk-averse benchmarks, outperforming standard CVaR-PG and recent competitive baselines (PCVaR-PG, RET-CAP) in both convergence speed and asymptotic performance.
Very clear presentation, detailed pseudocode, and thorough proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The algorithm introduces several complex components (e.g., tracking dynamic quantile levels at execution time, designing a monotonic network to prevent quantile crossing, scheduling the trade-off parameter), which increases implementation difficulty.
The scheduling of the trade-off parameter (e.g., decaying it to 0 at different phases of training depending on the task) seems highly heuristic and domain-dependent.

The empirical evaluation is limited to relatively low-dimensional control and grid-world tasks (Maze, LunarLander, Inverted Pendulum); scaling to more complex continuous control environments remains to be demonstrated.
